title: The ending -ni: the specific object
goal: Recognize when an object needs *-ni* and when it stands bare — a difference English shows with *the* versus *a*, and Uzbek shows with an ending.
bekal: put the required *-ni* on names, pronouns, and things already mentioned

dialogs.title: Dialog — Kitobni topa olmayapman
dialogs.intro: In the university library. Budi is rummaging through his bag in a panic.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Nilufar, have you seen my book?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Yes, the dictionary. I put it on the table this morning.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Men bir lugʻat koʻrdim, lekin sizniki emas edi.
lines.id: I saw a dictionary, but it wasn't yours.
lines.literal: I one dictionary saw-I, but yours not was.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Farqi bor: mening lugʻatim eski va qizil.
lines.id: There's a difference: my dictionary is old and red.
lines.literal: difference-its there-is: my dictionary-my old and red.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Unda anavi javonni koʻring. Men Anvarni chaqiraman.
lines.id: Then look at the shelf over there. I'll call Anvar.
lines.literal: that-over-there shelf-the look. I Anvar-the call-I.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: The librarian. He knows every book.

lines.speaker: Anvar:
lines.text: Qizil lugʻatmi? Uni men oldim — muqovasi yirtiq edi.
lines.id: A red dictionary? I took it — its cover is torn.
lines.literal: red dictionary-? it-the I took-I — cover-its torn is.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Voy, rahmat! Sizni butun kun qidirdim!
lines.id: Oh, thank you! I've been looking for you all day!
lines.literal: oh, thanks! you-the whole day searched-I!

lines.speaker: Anvar:
lines.id: You're welcome. Next time, don't leave books on the table!

notes: **Lugʻatni, not lugʻat.** In the third line Budi uses *-ni* because both of them know which dictionary is meant — it was just mentioned. In the fourth line Nilufar uses bare *lugʻat* because what she saw was *a* dictionary, not necessarily *the* one.
**Names and pronouns always take -ni.** *Anvarni chaqiraman* (I'll call Anvar), *Sizni qidirdim* (I was looking for you). A person is never "just any" — you always call a specific person.
**Uni = "it/him/her" as an object.** The *-ni* form of *u*. The full set: *meni* (me), *seni*, *uni*, *bizni*, *sizni*, *ularni*. Notice that *men* and *sen* shorten to *me-* and *se-*.
**Edi marks a past state.** *Sizniki emas edi* = "it wasn't yours (back then)". It's the past partner of the verbless sentences from unit 1, and it's explained in full in unit 11.

grammars.title: When to use -ni, and when not
body: English shows this with *the* and *a*. Uzbek has no articles, so it marks the specific object with an ending instead. The rule comes down to one question: **does the listener know exactly which thing I mean?**

head: Sentence
Meaning
Why
rows: any book — an activity, not a particular thing
the book we've already talked about
the tea in front of you
it has an owner → definitely specific

after: **Four things always take -ni:** proper names, personal pronouns, nouns with a possessive ending, and nouns pointed out with *bu/shu/u*. If any of these is there, don't hesitate — add *-ni*.

**What doesn't take -ni** is a non-specific object standing right before the verb and almost merging with it: *kitob oʻqimoq* (book-reading), *choy ichmoq* (tea-drinking), *ish qilmoq* (to work). English does something similar in "book-reading" or "to go shopping": one activity, not one particular object.
⚠️ Once the object **moves away from the spot right before the verb**, it almost always needs *-ni*: *Kitobni men oʻqiyman* (That book — I'm the one reading it).

grammars.title: Ending order: plural → possessive → object
body: Uzbek endings line up in a fixed order and never overtake each other. Once you know the order, you can take apart a word of any length.
after: The order **never** changes: base word → *-lar* → possessive ending → case ending. The same rule applies to *-da*, *-ga*, and *-dan*, which you have learned or will learn.

The most helpful practice isn't memorizing tables but **taking apart** long words you come across. Look at *doʻstlarimizda* and split it: *doʻst-lar-imiz-da* = "at our friends'". Five seconds, and the word stops being scary.

blocks.text: They're all adjectives, so they all stand in front of the noun and never change form.

⚠️ *Koʻk* means **blue**, but also **sky** and **light green** for plants: *koʻk choy* is green tea, not blue tea. Old Turkic didn't separate blue from green, and traces of that habit are still visible here.
*Jigarrang* literally means "liver-colored" (*jigar* = liver, a Persian word), and *kulrang* means "ash-colored". The ending *-rang* comes from Persian and means "color".
Ten question words cover almost all A1 conversation. Notice that they can all take endings, just like ordinary nouns: *kimga* (to whom), *nimada* (in what), *qayerdan* (from where).

⚠️ Uzbek question words **don't move anything**. A question is built exactly like a statement, with the verb still at the end: *Siz qayerda ishlaysiz?* Compare English, which has to flip the word order.
